ports_basics.title: Network Ports
ports_basics.body:
[b]A port is a numbered doorway on a host.[/b]

TCP and UDP multiplex services with 16-bit port numbers (0–65535). Well-known ports 0–1023 are reserved: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP.

In Level Blue, hostile packets are traffic aimed at a service. Closing unused ports shrinks the attack surface. Your towers are controls on those doors — they inspect, delay, or drop traffic before it reaches the keep.

[b]Remember:[/b] a listening port is an invitation. If you do not need the service, do not expose the port.

firewalls_intro.title: Firewall Fundamentals
firewalls_intro.body:
[b]A firewall is a policy enforcement point.[/b]

It sits on a trust boundary and allows, denies, or rate-limits packets using rules: source, destination, port, and protocol. Default-deny is safer than default-allow. Stateful inspection tracks whether a packet belongs to an established session.

The Scanner is that control in miniature: high fire rate, low damage — it inspects packets fast and buys time for stronger nodes to finish the job.

[b]Remember:[/b] a firewall is only as good as its rules. An allow-any rule is an open gate with extra paperwork.

crypto_101.title: Encryption Basics
crypto_101.body:
[b]Cryptography protects confidentiality and integrity in transit and at rest.[/b]

Symmetric ciphers (AES) use one shared secret. Asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECC) uses a key pair so you can publish a public key. TLS wraps HTTP so port 443 is not plaintext 80.

Hashing is not encryption: SHA-256 fingerprints data; you cannot reverse it to recover the original. The Sandbox is the combat metaphor — it contains traffic and slows it, because an isolated payload cannot sprint to the keep.

[b]Remember:[/b] never invent your own crypto. Use vetted libraries, rotate keys, and keep plaintext off the wire.
